Perspectives on, Substcinticbl Evidence—Biestek v. Berryhill. Supreme 
Court opinions elaborating on the substantial evidence standard are 
uncommon, if only because the Court rarely reviews fact-bound apphcations of 
general standards of review. In 2019, however, the Court addressed the scope 
of review under a Social Security statute providing that “the findingfl of the 
Commissioner of Social Security as to any fact, if supported by substantial 
evidence, shall be conclusive.” 42 U.S.C. § 405(g). See Biestek v. Berryhill, 587 
U.S. 97 (2019).
Writing for the Court, Justice Kagan held that the Social Security 
Administration’s rehance on an expert’s testimony about the availability of 
certain jobs in the economy could qualify as “substantial evidence,” even 
though the expert “largely based her opinion on private market-survey data” 
unavailable to the appHcant for benefits. She began her analysis by observing 
that “[t]he phrase ‘substantial evidence’ is a ‘term of art’ used throughout 
administrative law to describe how courts are to review agency factfinding” 
Relying on the Court’s 1938 opinion in Consolidated Edison, Justice Kagan 
reasoned that substantial evidence is “ ‘more than a mere scintilla^ ” and means 
“ ‘such relevant evidence as a reasonable mind might accept as adequate to 
support a conclusion.’ ” The Court ultimately rejected a “categorical rule, 
applying to every case in which a vocational expert refuses a request for 
underlying data”—^thereby holding that whether such expert testimony 
qualifies as substantial evidence must be assessed on a case-by-case basis.
In dissent. Justice Gorsuch claimed that “[t]he principle that the 
government must support its allegations with substantial evidence, not 
conclusions and secret evidence, guards against arbitrary executive 
decisionmaking.” Ultimately, however, the dispute between majority and 
dissent was narrow. Justice Gorsuch concluded that, under the facts of 
Biestek’s case, the expert’s testimony did not qualify as substantial evidence. 
The majority did not reach that question, but only rejected the categorical rule 
that expert testimony based on facts unavailable to a private party may never 
qualify as substantial evidence.
